title: “Bunker Busters”: Deep Targets, Shallow Stocks
gist: CSIS argues demand for bunker-buster munitions is rising because adversaries are tunneling deeper, the FY2027 budget request jumps to $429 million, and the 5,000 lb and 30,000 lb inventories are thin while Iran's deepest sites may be beyond reach.

insights.claim: The proposed FY 2027 defense budget requests $429 million for conventional bunker buster weapons, up from an average of $123 million (in FY 2027 dollars) over the previous 10 fiscal years.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Procurement tailwind for penetrator bomb and guidance-kit makers.
insights.quote: requesting $429 million for conventional bunker buster weapons
insights.locator: Out of the Shadows, Into the Mainstream

insights.claim: Hard and deeply buried targets are growing in number and hardness as countries and nonstate actors seek protection against U.S. precision weaponry, a trend colleague Eliot Cohen calls a revolution in tunneling affairs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sustained structural demand for penetrating munitions.
insights.locator: Out of the Shadows, Into the Mainstream

insights.claim: The United States needs bunker busters for two target sets: a large number of tunnels and moderately hard targets requiring volume, and a smaller set of facilities inside mountains where depth of penetration matters more than numbers.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Argues for both volume production and deep-penetration R&D.
insights.locator: Out of the Shadows, Into the Mainstream

insights.claim: Continuing Iranian missile launches suggest underground missile and drone storage facilities have survived, particularly among reportedly 33 underground missile bases adjacent to the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Implies further strike requirements and extended conflict risk around Hormuz.

insights.claim: Pickaxe Mountain, an Iranian nuclear site deeper than Isfahan or Natanz, is likely beyond the reach of even the most powerful conventional munitions, though construction is ongoing.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Fully preventing Iran's nuclear weapon capability may require nuclear or new deep-penetration options.

insights.claim: The United States retains a large inventory of 2,000 lb bunker busters but inventory stress may occur with the 5,000 lb munitions needed for the surviving, likely most hardened targets.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Replenishment orders for 5,000 lb penetrators are likely.

insights.claim: Fourteen GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrators were used in the attacks on Fordow and Natanz during Operation Midnight Hammer; the administration reprogrammed $123 million to replenish, deliveries will take years, and remaining MOPs are estimated in the low single digits.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Near-term scarcity of the heaviest conventional penetrator limits strike options.
insights.quote: The number of MOPs remaining in the U.S. inventory is estimated to be in the low single digits.

insights.claim: Israel has used large numbers of U.S.-made bunker busters in its wars since October 7, and Hamas's estimated 310 miles of tunnels, about six times the underground length of the Washington Metro, helped it survive attacks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Also drives demand on the U.S. supply base.

insights.claim: Current bunker busters are nearly all bombs requiring aircraft to fly over the target, which needs local air superiority that may not be achievable in a conflict with China, so a standoff munition is highly desirable.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Standoff penetrator development is a capability gap and a potential new program.
insights.locator: Out of the Shadows, Into the Mainstream

insights.claim: The JSOW-C is the only standoff hardened-target munition remaining; it glides 12 to 70 miles, the initial inventory goal was 7,000, Navy procurement ended after FY 2015 and several hundred are estimated to remain.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The BLU-138 5,000 lb A5K penetrator has been procured since FY 2023 and will replace the BLU-113/122, while the BLU-137 A2K is the latest 2,000 lb penetrator, procured since FY 2018.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Only a handful of 1.2 MT B83-1 nuclear bunker busters remain; the Biden administration planned to retire it, the Trump administration has not stated a policy, and Air Force budget materials suggest a new nuclear bunker buster may be in development.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Nuclear earth-penetrator policy is an open question.

insights.claim: China's PLA Rocket Force built tunnel networks, the Underground Great Wall, to protect its until recently limited nuclear arsenal and ensure second-strike capability, and many North Korean nuclear and missile facilities are underground.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Hardened targets are not only an Iran problem.
insights.locator: Out of the Shadows, Into the Mainstream
